Learning Objectives
Interpret the structure, composition, and biomechanical properties of tendon, ligament, and
enthesis.
Assess factors to be considered in mechanically testing tendons, ligaments, and enthesis.
Describe the development, injury, and healing processes of tendon, ligament, and enthesis.
Tendons
Overview
Function—Tendons transfer force from muscle to bone to produce joint motion and assist in
dynamic joint stabilization.

Tendons may be classified by shape (round or flat), anatomic location (intra-articular or extra-
articular), or by the surrounding layer of connective tissue (paratenon or synovium).
Structure and Composition
Tendon has a hierarchical structure (Figure 1) and is made up of densely packed collagen
fibers and water, with trace amounts of proteoglycans and elastin (Resource 1).
Type I collagen is the major constituent of tendon, making up approximately 86% of its dry
weight.
Type III collagen also is present in tendons and consists of approximately 5% of total collagen
content.
Proteoglycans make up 1% to 5% of the dry weight of a tendon.
Decorin is the predominant proteoglycan in tendon.
Aggrecan (a proteoglycan abundant in articular cartilage) is found in areas of tendon that are
under compression (eg, regions of hand flexor tendons that wrap around bone).
Elastin constitutes 1% to 5% of the dry weight of tendon and is important for resisting shear
force and small tensile stretch (less than 5% of total length).
The fibroblast is the predominant cell type in tendon.
Tendons are relatively hypovascular compared with many other organs; however, vascularity
varies depending on tendon type and locally within a tendon.
Figure 1 Illustration of a tendon. Tendon has a hierarchical structure, with collagen molecules
assembled into progressively larger bundles, until the level of the tendon itself is reached. Note

the neurovasculature of the tendon. (Reproduced from Counihan MM, Soslowsky LJ: Tendons and


Structure and Composition
The primary structure of collagen consists of glycine (33%), proline (15%), and
hydroxyproline (15%). The collagen molecule is fibrillar in structure, with a length of 300
nm and a diameter of 1.5 nm.
Collagen molecules are arranged in quarter-stagger arrays. Five collagen molecules form
an ordered microfibril unit. Microfibrils combine to form fibrils. Fibril units then form
highly ordered parallel bundles oriented in the direction of muscle force. Fibrils
accumulate to form fascicle units, which in turn combine to form the tendon. Endotenon
surrounds fascicles, and the entire tendon is surrounded by epitenon (also known as
paratenon), which is believed to harbor progenitor cells that may play a role in tendon
healing and remodeling.
Decorin is a small leucine-rich proteoglycan that regulates collagen fiber diameter by
inhibiting lateral fusion. Decorin molecules form cross-links between collagen fibers.
Therefore, the molecules have been hypothesized to transfer loads between collagen
fibers, thereby increasing the stiffness of the tendon; however, recent experimental
evidence has disputed this hypothesis.
Elastic fibers behave similar to springs and are abundant in tissues that commonly
experience cyclic stretch (eg, arterial walls, lungs, skin, and tendons). Elastin is primarily
found between collagen fascicles and the pericellular niche.
In longitudinal histologic sections, fibroblasts appear spindle-shaped, with a preferred
orientation in the direction of collagen fibers. In cross-section, fibroblasts are star-
shaped, with long cytoplasmic processes. Tendon fibroblasts are hypothesized to arise
from a common mesenchymal progenitor pool, known as tendon stem/progenitor cells.
Traditionally, terminally differentiated tendon fibroblasts were believed to be SEND FEEDBACK

3/21

phenotypically homogeneous; however, single-cell RNA sequencing has revealed at least
five transcriptionally distinct cell phenotypes in adult tendons.
Sheathed tendons (eg, flexor tendons of the hand) have regions that are relatively
avascular. The crescent of the rotator cuff and the region marked by the rotator cable (a
band of transversely oriented fibers from the coracohumeral ligament) also are
hypovascular. This also is the location at which the rotator cuff most frequently tears.
These regions receive nutrition via diffusion from the synovium. Tendons not enclosed
by a sheath receive their blood supply from vessels entering from the tendon surface or
from the tendon enthesis (the tendon-to-bone insertion).
Development
Developing tendon is highly cellular and becomes less cellular during postnatal growth.
The morphology of tendon cells in mature tendon typically are elongated in the direction of
loading, parallel to collagen fibrils.
Major transcription factors associated with tendon development include Scleraxis (recruitment
of mesenchymal progenitors) and SRY-box transcription factor 9 (at the tendon enthesis).
Expression of both transcription factors is found in other tissues/cell types, including cartilage;
however, Scleraxis is expressed by all tendon progenitors and cells.
Biomechanics
Tendons have high tensile properties and buckle under compression (rope-like behavior).
The intrinsic mechanical properties of tendon vary depending on the direction of loading;
therefore, tendon is an anisotropic material.
Tendon biomechanics can be characterized by structural properties (load-elongation behavior)
or material properties (stress-strain behavior).
Tendons are viscoelastic and, therefore, exhibit time-dependent mechanical properties.
Several factors influence the biomechanical properties of tendons.
Anatomic location
Genetics
Activity level
Age

Biomechanics
Tendons exhibit high tensile strength parallel to the primary collagen fiber axis and low
tensile strength perpendicular to the primary collagen fiber axis. Conversely, materials
with the same mechanical properties in all directions are known as isotropic (eg, glass or
metals).
A typical load-elongation curve for tendon includes toe, linear, and failure regions
(Figure 2). Structural properties describe the overall load-bearing capacity of the tissue
and include the contribution of the muscle and bone attachments and the geometry of
the tissue (cross-sectional area and length). Structural properties include stiffness (the
slope of the linear portion of the curve in Figure 2) and failure load. Material properties
(also referred to as mechanical properties) describe the quality of the tissue. Material
properties are calculated by obtaining the engineering stress and strain, which normalize
load and elongation to account for tissue geometry. Stress is calculated by dividing load
by cross-sectional area, and strain is calculated by dividing change in elongation by initial
length.
Material properties include the modulus of elasticity (the linear relationship between
stress and strain, observed as the slope of the linear region of the stress-strain curve),
failure stress (ie, strength), and toughness (energy absorbed before rupture).
Viscoelastic materials display elastic and viscous behavior. In tendon, elastic behavior is
primarily driven by the spring-like performance of collagen and elastin. Viscous behavior
is primarily attributed to electrostatic and hydrogen binding of proteoglycans to joint
fluid, fluid movement through the dense matrix, and molecular rearrangement. These
phenomena result in the following observed behaviors:

Hysteresis: dependence on loading history (Figure 2)
Creep: increase in strain over time for a constant applied stress (Figure 2).
Stress relaxation: decrease in stress over time for a constant applied strain
(Figure 2).
Tendons from different anatomic locations have different structural properties (eg,
digital flexor tendons have twice the failure load of digital extensor tendons. The
insertion of a tendon just distal to a joint allows the tendon to act as a buttress against
translation of the articular surfaces (eg, hamstring acting as a secondary stabilizer for the
anterior cruciate ligament [ACL]).
Mutations in genes that encode for extracellular matrix protein synthesis, structure, and
cross-linking may affect tendon mechanical properties in minor and major ways (eg,
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome).
Exercise has a positive effect that leads to increased turnover of type I collagen. Training
can promote synthesis and degradation of collagen, especially type I collagen, and
decrease collagen cross-linking. Immobilization has a detrimental effect on the
biomechanical and structural properties of healthy tendons. In vivo, cast immobilization
leads to decreased tensile strength and stiffness and total weight of tendon. In vitro,
tendons and ligaments require tensile loads to maintain their collagen fiber alignment
and strength. Immobilization also results in decreased cellularity, reduced collagen
organization, and smaller collagen fibril diameter.
The material and structural properties of tendons increase from birth through maturity.
The properties then decrease from maturity through old age. Collagen cross-linking
accumulates with maturation. Aging leads to accumulation of advanced glycation end
products, which reduces tissue toughness.

Mechanical Testing
The following factors should be considered in mechanically testing ligaments:
Tendon mechanical properties vary with hydration, temperature, and pH. They must be
tested under physiologically relevant hydration, temperature, and pH conditions.

The high strength and lubricated surfaces of tendons make it difficult to grip during
mechanical testing. Specialized grips (eg, freeze clamps) may be necessary to prevent the
tendon from slipping out of the grip.
Measurement of tissue cross-sectional area is necessary to calculate stress (stress =
load/cross-sectional area). Care must be taken in measuring the cross-sectional area of
tendon because the tissue will deform if contact methods (eg, calipers) are used.
Because tendons are viscoelastic (ie, their properties are time-dependent), the rate at which
the tendon is pulled may influence the mechanical properties. Higher strain rates result in a
higher elastic modulus.
Specimens should be stored frozen and hydrated. Improper storage may affect the
mechanical properties of the tendon.
The orientation of a tendon during testing will influence the mechanical properties measured
(eg, the structural properties of the supraspinatus tendon depend on the angle of the
humeral head relative to the glenoid).
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Tendon injury results from direct trauma (eg, laceration of a flexor tendon) or indirect tensile
overload (eg, Achilles tendon rupture). Several tendinopathies (eg, rotator cuff degeneration)
may predispose tendons to chronic accumulation of damage.
Three overlapping phases of tendon healing occur.
Hemostasis/inflammation
Cell proliferation and extracellular matrix production
Remodeling/maturation
Modulation of tendon repair via anti-inflammatory drugs has been controversial.
Some antibiotic agents (eg, fluoroquinolone) are known to increase the risk of spontaneous
tendon rupture caused by degenerative microscopic changes to tendon.
Long-term effects—The structural properties of repaired tendons typically reach only two-
thirds of normal, even 1 year after repair. Material property differences may be even more
pronounced.
The two critical considerations for sheathed tendon healing are prevention of adhesion
formation and accrual of mechanical strength (Figure 3).
Tendons not enclosed in sheaths fail because of trauma (eg, an acute sports injury) or
preexisting pathology (eg, a rotator cuff tear after years of chronic tendon degeneration).

Sheathed tendons: flexor tendons of the hand often are injured via direct trauma (eg,
laceration).
Intra-articular tendons and ligaments (eg, rotator cuff and ACL) tend to have poor intrinsic
healing capacity and frequently require surgical management if injured.
Therapeutic modalities include local biologic agents, phonophoresis, extracorporeal
shockwave treatment, and dry needling.
The role of rehabilitation during healing is complex and dependent on the injury and timing
after surgical repair.
Figure 3 Illustration shows extrinsic and intrinsic healing processes in a sheathed tendon.
Adhesions may result from activation of the extrinsic process, inhibiting tendon gliding within the
synovial sheath. (Adapted with permission from Gelberman RH, Vande Berg JS, Lundborg GN,
Akeson WH: Flexor tendon healing and restoration of the gliding surface: An ultrastructural study
in dogs. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1983;65[1]:70-80.)

Injury, Repair, and Healing
Postinjury, the wound site is infiltrated by inflammatory cells. Platelets aggregate at the
wound and create a fibrin clot to stabilize the torn tendon edges. Neutrophils and
macrophages migrate to the wound site and release chemotactic factors to recruit other
cells, such as fibroblasts. During this phase of healing, tendon is at its weakest. The
length of this phase is on the order of days, typically lasting as long as 1 week
(Videos 1 and 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:46 AM
AAOS | Tendon and Ligament Biology and Biomechanics

Fibroblasts infiltrate the wound site and proliferate. They produce extracellular matrix,
including large amounts of type I and type III collagen. The injury response in adult
tendon is scar-mediated (ie, large amounts of disorganized collagen are deposited at the
repair site) rather than regenerative. The length of this phase is on the order of weeks.
The predominant growth factors present during this phase include transforming growth
factor-beta, insulin-like growth factor-1, vascular endothelial growth factor, platelet-
derived growth factor, and basic fibroblast growth factor.
Matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) degrade the collagen matrix, replacing type III
collagen with type I collagen. MMP-9 and MMP-13 primarily participate in collagen
degradation, whereas MMP-2, MMP-3, and MMP-14 participate in degradation and
remodeling. Collagen fibers are reorganized so they are aligned in the direction of
muscle loading. The length of this phase is on the order of months to years.
In preclinical models, prolonged use of systemic NSAIDs has been shown to delay
healing and result in weaker tendons after surgical repair. The mechanism that drives
this is unknown. Strategies are being developed to target specific signaling pathways
and/or localized and sustained drug delivery to improve healing outcomes.
Non-sheathed tendons have a greater capacity to heal than sheathed tendons. Injury
often occurs at the attachments of the tendon (ie, at the tendon-to-bone insertion or at
the musculotendinous junction).
This is hypothesized to be because of synovial fluid, matrix-degrading proteases, and the
inability to form a fibrin clot to serve as a provisional scaffold for healing. Conversely,
extra-articular tendons and ligaments (eg, Achilles tendon and medial collateral ligament
[MCL]) have been shown to heal well without surgical management. Some ligaments
have a relatively high vascular supply compared with other ligaments/tendons (eg,
posterior cruciate ligament [PCL]), which may improve healing outcomes.
Local biologic agents to promote microcirculation may be effective for improving patient
outcomes. Examples of local biologic agents include topical nonsteroidal anti-
inflammatory agents, nitroglycerin, leukocyte-rich platelet-rich plasma, and cell therapy.
Phonophoresis is the use of therapeutic ultrasonography to drive medication delivery.
SEND FEEDBACK

Extracorporeal shockwave treatment induces microscopic tissue injury that improves
microcirculation. Dry needling induces microscopic tissue injury that is thought to
stimulate healing; however, no consensus exists with regard to such outcomes. Tendon
needling has been shown to improve patient-reported outcomes for Achilles tendon,
rotator cuff, and lateral epicondylitis; however, limited high-quality, evidence-based
studies are available to support its widespread use.
Protective immobilization in the early period after tendon repair may be beneficial in
many scenarios (eg, after rotator cuff repair). Active loading, including exercise, may be
detrimental if initiated too early in the rehabilitation period but is beneficial during the
remodeling phase of healing. Early passive motion is beneficial for flexor tendon healing.
Early motion suppresses adhesion formation between the tendon and the sheath,
preventing the typical range-of-motion losses observed with immobilized tendons.

Ligaments
Overview
Function—Ligaments guide joint kinematics and stabilize joints by restricting motion between
bones.
Ligaments are classified according to anatomic location of their attachment to bone. Capsular
ligaments are found within the articular capsule of synovial joints. Extracapsular ligaments are
associated with synovial joints but are separate from the articular capsule.
Structure and Composition
Similar to tendons, ligaments have a highly ordered hierarchical structure; however, the
collagen fibers in ligaments are less organized than those in tendons.
Ligaments typically are shorter and wider than tendons.
Ligaments are composed of densely packed collagen fibers, proteoglycans, elastin, and water.
The total collagen content of ligaments is slightly lower than that of tendon.

Type I collagen makes up approximately 70% of the dry weight of ligaments.
The collagen fibers in ligaments are less organized than that in tendons.
Similar to tendons, the main cell type in ligaments is the fibroblast, but ligament fibroblasts
appear rounder than tendon fibroblasts.
Ligament structure varies between anatomic location depending on their interaction with joint
synovial fluid. Intra-articular ligaments (eg, ACL) possess less biologic activity and healing
capacity compared with extra-articular ligaments (eg, MCL).
Ligaments have relatively low vascularity, innervation, and cellularity.

Structure and Composition
The vasculature is primarily restricted to the epiligamentous plexus surrounding the
ligament. Sensory nerve endings near the ligament insertion site function as nociceptive
pain sensors and proprioceptive position sensors, both contributing to the stability of
the joint via effects on muscle function and resultant joint kinematics.
Biomechanics
Similar to tendons, ligaments have high tensile properties and buckle under compression
(rope-like behavior).
The intrinsic mechanical properties of ligament vary depending on the direction of loading;
therefore, ligaments are an anisotropic material.
For example, they exhibit high tensile strength parallel to the primary collagen fiber axis and
low tensile strength perpendicular to the primary collagen fiber axis.
Basic biomechanical properties are similar between tendon and ligament.

Factors Influencing the Biomechanical Properties of Ligaments
Ligaments from different anatomic locations have different structural properties. The
material and structural properties of ligaments increase from birth through maturity.
The properties then decrease from maturity through old age. Skeletally immature
specimens undergo avulsion-type failure, whereas older specimens are associated with a
higher incidence of midsubstance failure.
Mutations in genes that encode for extracellular matrix protein synthesis, structure, and
cross-linking may affect ligament mechanical properties in minor and major ways (eg,
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome).
Exercise increases the structural properties of ligaments, including strength and
stiffness. Similar to tendons, immobilization has a detrimental effect on the
biomechanical and structural properties of ligaments. Immobilization results in
decreased cellularity, reduced collagen organization, smaller collagen fibril diameter,
and decreased mechanical properties.
Damage to the ACL is two to eight times more likely in females than males. This has been
hypothesized to be, in part, the result of increased dynamic valgus and abduction loads
experienced by females during activity, which may be because of neuromuscular control
factors. In addition, differences in hormone levels are believed to influence intrinsic
ligament properties. Although estrogen does not have a substantial effect on ligaments,
the hormone relaxin does decrease collagen synthesis and may reduce mechanical
properties.
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Ligament injuries generally are classified into three grades: I, II, and III. Grade I injuries
correspond with a mild sprain, grade II injuries correspond with a moderate sprain/partial tear,
and grade III injuries correspond with a complete ligament tear. An additional type of injury is
avulsion of the ligament from its bony insertion.

Ligament healing occurs via the same phases as tendon healing: hemostasis/inflammation,
matrix and cell proliferation, and remodeling/maturation.
Early in the healing process of ligaments, a higher proportion of type III collagen fibers relative
to type I collagen fibers exists. This ratio returns to normal in approximately 1 year; however,
only approximately 45% of the mature collagen cross-links are present compared with the
original ligament.
Extra-articular ligaments (eg, the MCL of the knee) have a greater capacity to heal than intra-
articular ligaments (eg, the ACL of the knee).
PCL of the knee—Midsubstance PCL injuries have variable healing capacity. Surgical
reconstruction of the PCL often is necessary to restore stability in the injured knee.

Injury, Repair, and Healing
Autografts, including bone-patellar tendon-bone, semitendinosus, quadriceps, and
gracilis, commonly are used. The structural properties of the reconstructed graft attain
only approximately 50% of normal properties at the longest follow-up studied. The major
disadvantage of autografts is donor-site morbidity. Allograft tendon also is used for ACL
reconstruction. Disadvantages of allografts include the potential for disease
transmission, the possible detrimental effects of the graft processing and sterilization
process on mechanical properties, and a prolonged inflammatory process compared
with autografts. A process described as ligamentization occurs in autografts and
allografts after ACL reconstruction. The traditional understanding is that autograft
fibroblasts undergo necrosis soon after reconstruction and are replaced by host-derived
fibroblasts; however, this is based on animal studies, most of which are failed
reconstruction procedures with residual laxity. In that setting, stress deprivation of the
ACL graft occurs, which may affect the biologic events. Limited human biopsy specimens
suggest that a subset of intrinsic fibroblasts in the donor tendon graft may survive
transplantation. Similarly, allografts are infiltrated by host-derived fibroblasts in the early
period after implantation. Both types of grafts may undergo some elongation during the
remodeling phase because of creep of the graft material.

Enthesis
Overview
Function—Tendons and ligaments insert into bone across a complex transitional tissue known
as the enthesis. Microscale changes in extracellular matrix composition and structural
organization prevent stress concentrations that would naturally arise from attaching tissues
with dissimilar material properties (tendon/ligament to bone).
Entheses are classified according to the type of insertion (ie, direct versus indirect;
fibrocartilage versus fibrous).
Structure and Composition
Indirect insertions (eg, the femoral insertion of the MCL) have a superficial layer that connects
with the periosteum and a deep layer that anchors to bone via Sharpey fibers. These are
primarily fibrous insertions.
Direct insertions (eg, the supraspinatus insertion of the rotator cuff) classically have been
categorized into four zones: tendon/ligament proper, uncalcified fibrocartilage, calcified
fibrocartilage, and subchondral bone.
Although the insertion site typically is categorized into zones, changes in the tissue are graded,
without distinct borders between zones (Figure 4). This graded transition in tissue composition
is presumed to aid in the efficient transfer of load between tendon and bone.

Structure and Composition
First zone (tendon/ligament proper)—The properties in this zone are similar to those at
the tissue midsubstance. It consists of well-aligned type I collagen fibers with lesser
amounts of the proteoglycan decorin. The cell type in this zone is the fibroblast.
Second zone (fibrocartilage)—This zone marks the beginning of the transition from
tendinous material to bony material. It is composed of type II and type III collagen, with
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:46 AM
AAOS | Tendon and Ligament Biology and Biomechanics
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001152
17/21

lesser amounts of type I, type IX, and type X collagen and lesser amounts of the
proteoglycans aggrecan and decorin. The cell type in this zone is the fibrochondrocyte.
Third zone (mineralized fibrocartilage)—This zone is characterized by a marked
transition toward bony tissue. The predominant collagen is type II, with considerable
amounts of type X collagen and aggrecan. The cell types in this zone are the
fibrochondrocyte and the hypertrophic chondrocyte.
Fourth zone (bone)—This zone predominantly is made up of type I collagen with a high
mineral content. The cell types in this zone are the osteoblast, the osteocyte, and the
osteoclast.
The mineral in the enthesis appears distinct on non-decalcified histologic sections.
Biomechanics
A functionally graded transition between tendon and bone is necessary to reduce stress
concentrations at the interface of two tissues with different material properties
(tendon/ligament and bone).
The enthesis typically has lower mechanical properties in tension than the tendon or ligament
midsubstance. This compliant region between tendon/ligament and bone reduces stress
concentrations that would otherwise arise between the dissimilar materials and creates a
tough attachment.
Mechanical loading is critical for the functional development of the tendon enthesis.

Biomechanics
Composition grading is evident in mineral content and proteoglycan content, structural
grading is evident in collagen fiber organization, and mechanical grading is evident in
elastic and viscoelastic properties. Absence or loss of muscle loading during critical
stages of tendon/enthesis growth leads to reduced mineralization, decreased strength
and toughness, and smaller fibrocartilage regions at the tendon-bone attachment, as

well as smaller bone ridges at the location at which tendons attach to bone (eg,
tuberosities, tubercles). The mechanoresponsive behavior of enthesis progenitor cells
recently has been shown to be dependent on hedgehog signaling. Factors that
mechanistically drive changes in enthesis growth in response to increased muscle
loading remain unknown.
Injury, Repair, and Healing
Tendon-to-bone and ligament-to-bone healing are necessary in several scenarios.
Rotator cuff injuries, which comprise most of the soft-tissue injuries to the upper extremity,
commonly require surgical repair of the tendons to the humeral head.
Most ACL reconstruction techniques involve the use of tendon grafts that must heal in tibial
and femoral bone tunnels.
Avulsion injuries to the flexor tendons of the hand require tendon-to-bone repair.

Injury, Repair, and Healing
Clinical outcomes are variable in many cases of tendon-to-bone healing. The most
drastic feature of the failed healing response is lack of a transitional tissue between the
healing tendon and bone. The complex microstructure and composition of the native
enthesis is not reformed after surgical repair of tendon to bone. Rather, healing occurs
via the formation of a poorly organized, fibrovascular scar tissue.
Regeneration of the natural functionally graded interface between tendon and bone is
critical for the restoration of joint function and the prevention of reinjury.
Approaches for augmentation of tendon-bone healing include repairing structural
interface via scaffolds, possibly with the use of graded interface; modulating bone
metabolism via alendronate, parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, etc.; modulating the
extracellular remodeling process via doxycycline (modulates MMPs); and modulating
inflammation and immune response (eg, interleukin-17, Wnt signaling).
